title: Fast Pandas: Memory, Vectorisation and When to Switch
summary: Quick revision notes on shrinking pandas memory, replacing slow row-wise code with vectorised operations, how copy-on-write works in pandas 3, and when Polars or DuckDB is the better tool.

chapters.title: Memory Model and Measuring Usage
points: Mental model: a DataFrame is a set of typed column arrays (NumPy or Arrow-backed); memory cost = rows x dtype width per column, so dtype choice is the main lever
df.memory_usage() default is shallow: object columns count only 8-byte pointers, so strings look tiny and the number is wrong
df.memory_usage(deep=True) walks every Python object and counts real string bytes; use it (or df.info(memory_usage='deep')) before optimising
Default dtypes are wasteful: int64, float64, object (or str in pandas 3); a column of 5 repeated labels still stores every string
Workflow: measure with deep=True -> pick cheaper dtype per column -> convert -> re-measure and compare; sort columns by memory_usage(deep=True) to find the top offender

chapters.title: Shrinking Memory with Dtypes
points: pd.to_numeric(s, downcast='integer') picks the smallest int that fits (int8 -127..127, int16, int32); downcast='unsigned' for non-negative; downcast='float' gives float32
s.astype('int32') or 'float32' is the explicit form; check values fit first, since an overflow wraps silently in NumPy casts
Low-cardinality strings -> astype('category'): stores integer codes plus one lookup of uniques; large saving when unique count is far below row count
Nullable dtypes (Int64, Float64, 'string', 'boolean') hold missing values without falling back to float64 or object; convert_dtypes() infers them
Set dtypes at load time: read_csv(dtype={...}, usecols=[...]) or pd.read_parquet(columns=[...]) so the full-width frame is never built; float32 loses precision (~7 digits), so avoid it for money

chapters.title: Avoiding apply and iterrows
points: iterrows() builds a Series per row and upcasts mixed dtypes to one type, so it is slow and can silently change types; itertuples() is much faster if a loop is truly needed
df.apply(f, axis=1) and Series.apply(f) are Python-level loops calling f once per row/element; no C speed-up, only a convenient syntax
Never grow a DataFrame in a loop with concat or append per row; collect rows in a list and build once with pd.DataFrame(rows)
Vectorised ops run whole columns in compiled code, typically 10-100x faster than apply on large data
Profile before rewriting: %timeit on a sample or df.head(10000) shows whether the loop is the real bottleneck

chapters.title: Vectorised Alternatives
points: Arithmetic and comparisons on columns: df['total'] = df['price'] * df['qty']; boolean masks replace if/else per row
Conditional values: np.where(cond, a, b) for two branches; np.select([c1, c2], [v1, v2], default=v0) for many branches
Strings and dates via accessors: s.str.lower(), s.str.contains(), s.str.split(expand=True), s.dt.year, s.dt.dayofweek instead of apply with Python string/date code
Lookups and aggregates: s.map(dict) for value mapping, merge for joins, groupby().agg() or transform() for per-group math instead of looping over groups
Rolling and shifting: s.shift(), s.diff(), s.rolling(n).mean(), s.cumsum() replace index-based loops; for truly custom logic use numba or fall back to apply only on the small remainder

chapters.title: Copy-on-Write and Choosing Polars or DuckDB
points: Pandas 3 makes copy-on-write the only behaviour: any result of an operation behaves as a separate copy, and data is physically copied only when you modify it (lazy copy)
Chained assignment df['a'][mask] = 1 or df[mask]['a'] = 1 no longer modifies df; use df.loc[mask, 'a'] = 1 in one step. SettingWithCopyWarning is gone
In-place on a derived object never leaks back: y = x['a']; y.iloc[0] = 9 leaves x unchanged, so views are safe, and you no longer need defensive .copy() calls
Switch to Polars when you need multi-core speed, lazy query optimisation (scan_parquet, .lazy(), .collect()), expression API and lower memory on data around 1-100 GB

Switch to DuckDB when the work is SQL-shaped: duckdb.sql('select ... from df') queries pandas frames or Parquet files in place, runs out-of-core, and returns df via .df(); stay in pandas for small data, plotting and ecosystem (scikit-learn, matplotlib)

chapters.title: Pandas Performance Cheat Sheet
points: Measure: df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum(); df.info(memory_usage='deep')
Shrink: pd.to_numeric(s, downcast='integer'|'float'); s.astype('category'); read_csv(dtype=..., usecols=...); convert_dtypes()
Replace loops: iterrows/apply(axis=1) -> column math, np.where, np.select, .str, .dt, map, groupby.transform; if a loop is unavoidable use itertuples()
Write safely: df.loc[mask, col] = value; never chained indexing; no defensive .copy() needed in pandas 3
Tool choice: pandas = small and interactive; Polars = fast multi-core and lazy; DuckDB = SQL over files and frames, larger than memory
